The discussion of a subject of such importance as health insurance calls for placing before the house certain facts and considerations which have a serious bearing on the question and thus providing a proper orientation to any legislation which aims at supplying complete medical service to all the people of Canada. The Canadian Medical Association undertook to formulate such a plan as early as 1930. May I say briefly what the Canadian Medical Association is and means to the country?
In round figures there are 10,000 registered medical practitioners in Canada. They are grouped into various provincial medical societies, and these societies in practically every province are recognized as branches or divisions of the association. The business of the C.M.A., to use the abbreviation term of the Canadian Medical Association, is conducted through a council of approximately 120 representatives sent as delegates from the various provincial medical societies. These delegates in turn elect seventeen members to form the executive committee of the Canadian Medical Association, which carries on the affairs of the association during the year. The Canadian Medical Association meets once a year, generally in June, in annual session. The association as a body therefore represents and speaks for the medical profession of Canada; it is authorized to do so. One article of its constitution and by-laws includes the following
two items: first, the promotion of public health; second, the endeavour to assist in the advancement of medical legislation for the good of the public and the profession. Under these objects it would be fair to assume that the association is committed to engage itself actively in the consideration of plans whereby the state of the public health may be improved, also to consider ways and means of raising the standards and increasing the efficiency of medical practice in the common interest of the medical profession and of the public.
For this reason, namely, to improve the status of medical practice in Canada and to give better medical services, since 1930 the Canadian Medical Association has been making a thorough study of the question of health insurance. To that end, a committee was charged with the task of making a complete survey of health insurance in every country in the world as well as a complete study of all literature available on the subject. The committee on economics of the Canadian Medical Association was enlarged by a number of medical practitioners, the number being brought up to twenty-seven, with representation from every province in Canada. To implement and render more efficient the task which it imposed upon itself, it went as far as to send its general secretary to Europe to get first hand information on the question of health insurance as it is carried on in various countries which have adopted the system. The report of the secretary will be presented at the coming annual meeting of the Canadian Medical Association.
Prior to' that, in 1934, this committee on economics, charged with the special study of health insurance, presented a voluminous report of about forty pages, and my task tonight will be to endeavour to give the house, as briefly as possible at this advanced hour, a synopsis of the basic principles adopted by the committee on health insurance and approved by the Canadian Medical Association. With this object in view I shall quote extracts from the report in order to cover the ground as rapidly as possible, and in doing so I speak with the knowledge acquired as one of the members of the study committee of the Canadian Medical Association, who have been investigating health insurance since 1930. After reviewing legislation and literature, the report makes the following general observations :
In reviewing the causes which lead to a demand for health insurance, our committee recognized that there exists among the public considerable dissatisfaction with regard to the methods of medical practice. The expression of this dissatisfaction does not imply any

criticism of medicine or of the medical profession. Indeed it is the very contrary, because the dissatisfaction grows out of an appreciation of medicine and a desire to profit more fully by what medicine has to offer for the benefit of mankind.
The real problem arises out of the inability to pay for such medical services as are required. . . .
It would appear that the problem grows out of the following conditions:
1.	A change in our social organization under which the state has assumed increasing responsibility for the welfare of the citizens, as evidenced by legislation covering old age pensions, mothers' allowances, workmen's compensation, and so forth.
2.	The present individualistic system of medical practice is of long standing. It has not adjusted itself to the present social organization in which the majority are wage-earners with no resources beyond their weekly earnings.
3.	Medical facilities are not fairly distributed, and so some areas are deprived of essential medical services because the population of these areas is not sufficient to support the required medical services.
4.	The wage-earning population are often unable to pay ordinary fees, and are certainly not in a position to meet the costs of a long or serious illness. The wage-earner usually loses his wages when he is ill, at the very time when expenses are increased and the necessity continues for providing maintenance for his family.
5.	Medical care becomes a luxury rather than a necessity when the income provides only sufficient for food, shelter and clothing.
6.	The medical profession is expected to furnish medical care for the indigent-a state responsibility-without remuneration.
7.	Because of the cost of medical care, there is delay in securing care and a great deal of self-medication.
8.	Modern medicine is inevitably more costly, as seen in the development of hospitalization and specialist services.
9.	Modern medicine demands, in a percentage of eases, that consultant, hospital and other facilities be available if the patient is to receive the care required. This implies an actual correlation of existing services and making these services available to the patient through the family physician.
Our report is divided into three sections. The first reviews all health insurance legislation of other countries as well as all the literature that was available to us. Part II reviews the health legislation situation in Canada, and part III explains the Canadian Medical Association's plans for state health insurance in Canada. Here we are concerned chiefly with part II and part III. Part II reviews, first, the practise of medicine in Canada, its legal set-up and its development along individualistic lines; and, second, medical care as applied to the three groups of individuals who make up our population-the indigents, the middle class, and the well-to-do.

In supplying medical care to all three of these classes there are considerable deficiencies and shortcomings under the present system of medical practice. The medical care of the indigent is a distinct provincial or municipal responsibility as established by the British North America Act.
All provinces have made some provision for the medical care of this group of the population. Unfortunately, in general, the care of indigents in their own homes is left to the medical profession, although in some places a physician is paid out of public funds to give such care. When hospital care is required, a per capita per diem allowance is usually paid to the institution caring for the patient; but no fee is paid to the physician, it being argued iby some that the physician receives his reward through his hospital appointment. The medical profession is proud of its record of gratuitous service to those who are in need. The members of the profession in general are willing to give a certain amount of free service. Nevertheless, there is a general feeling that the profession is being exploited, and that governments are meeting their responsibilities for the care of the indigent at the expense of the medical profession. Free service should be entirely voluntary; but to assume that the medical profession will contribute one of the necessities of life, for the provision of which the state is responsible, is unsound in every way. It is interesting to note that physicians are not allowed to deduct from their taxable incomes, under the heading of contributions to charity, a sum equal to their free service.
In this connection, on the question of the treatment of indigents, may I add the following remarks. In New Brunswick there are 265 registered practitioners, or, to use round figures, let us say 250. In normal times there is not one physician in the province who each year does not perform at least $1,000 worth of medical work for which no entries are ever made in his books. That means a quarter of a million dollars' worth of free services given each year in ordinary times. During the time of the depression there was not one physician in the province who did not contribute at least $3,000 worth of services to the people of New Brunswick, -meaning a contribution of three quarters of a million dollars for New Brunswick alone, the smallest but one of the provinces. If we take the 10,000 registered practitioners in Canada, and allow that $2,000 was the minimum amount of free service which each contributed to the country every year during the depression period, it amounts to $20,000,000 each year,

State Medicine
and in the seven years of the depression it attains the enormous sum of about 8150,000,000 or approximately one-quarter of the entire amount spent by the federal, provincial and municipal governments to provide assistance to the unemployed.
Our committee has figures from the various provinces showing clearly that in ordinary times, outside contributions to hospitalization costs, provincial and municipal governments have not, in general, recognized their responsibility for the provision of medical care for the indigent. Furthermore it is regrettable to note that the federal government does not regard medical care as one of the necessities of life, otherwise medical care would have been provided for in the unemployment relief legislation, together with food, clothing and shelter.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the hour of closing rapidly approaches, so I shall be obliged to pass over many of the considerations which I wished to present to the house. However, I should like to place on record a series of resolutions adopted by the Canadian Medical Association showing what it considers the fundamental principles necessary to be recognized in any scheme of health legislation which might be enacted in Canada. These are as follows:
1.	That in the provinces where health insurance is established it be administered under an independent health insurance commission, and that there should be close cooperation between this commission and the provincial Department of Public Health with a view to making full use of preventive services.
2.	That a central health insurance board and local insurance boards be appointed, representative of all interested, to advise the responsible administrative authority.
3.	That the professional side of health insurance medical service be the responsibility of the organized medical profession through the appointment of a central medical services committee and local medical services committees to consider and advise on all questions affecting the administration of the medical benefit.
4.	That the question of the establishment of local areas for health insurance administration be left to the decision of the individual provinces.
5.	That the whole province be served by adequate departments of public health, organized on the basis of provision of individual health supervision by the health insurance general practitioner.
6.	That there be a health insurance fund, and that regional officers to act as supervisors and referees be appointed, paid and controlled by the central board or commission.
7.	That medical care for indigents be provided under the plan, the government to pay the premiums of the indigent, who then receive medical care under exactly the same conditions as the insured person.
8.	That the plan be compulsory for persons having an annual income below a level which upon investigation by competent local authorities proves to be insufficient to meet the costs of adequate medical care.
9.	That the dependents of insured persons be eligible for the medical benefits.
10.	That there be offered, on a voluntary basis, to those with incomes above the health insurance level, hospital care insurance, and that this be administered as part of the health insurance plan, such hospital care not to include medical service other than hospitalization.
11.	That the only benefit under the plan be the medical benefit.
12.	That the medical benefits be organized as follows-[DOT]
(a)	Every qualified licensed medical practitioner to be eligible to practise under the plan.
(b)	The insured person to have freedom of choice of medical practitioner and vice versa.
(c)	The medical service to be based upon making available to all a general practitioner service for health supervision and the treatment of disease.
(d)	Additional services to be secured ordinarily through the medical practitioner.
(1)	(a) Specialist medical service.
(b) Consultant medical service.
(2)	Yisiting-nurse service (in the home).
(3)	Hospital care.
(4)	Auxiliary services-usually in hospital.
(5)	Pharmaceutical service.
(e)	Dental service, arranged direct with dentist or upon reference.
13.	That the insurance fund should receive contributions from the insured, the employer of the insured and the government.
(a)	Payment of the premium of the insured in certain proportions to be determined, should be made by the employee, employer and government.
(b)	AYhere an. insured person has not an employer or where it is not practical for the government to collect from the employer the government should pay in for that insured person what would be the employer's share as well as its own share of the premium.
(e) Where the insured is "indigent" or has been out of work long enough to come without the scope of the provisions of the act as relating to an insured employee the government should assume payment of the full premium.
14.	That the medical practitioner of each province be remunerated according to the method or methods of payment which they select.
15.	(a) That the schedule of fees in any health insurance scheme shall be the schedule of fees accepted by the organized profession in the province concerned.
(b) That all schedules of fees be under complete control of the organized medical profession in each province.
16.	That the contract-salary service be limited to areas with a population insufficient to maintain a general practitioner in the area without additional support from the insurance fund.
17.	That no economic barrier be imposed between doctor and patient.
State Medicine

18.	That the volume of work demanded from and the remuneration to members of the various professions be such as to assure a standard of service equal to or better than present-day standards.
May I conclude with a summing-up as follows.
For the last ten years there has been a growing demand in certain sections of Canada for some form of health insurance.
Conscious of this trend of thought the Canadian Medical Association made a thorough, world-embracing investigation of health insurance.
With this study as a foundation it has formulated definite plans for health insurance, acceptable to both the general public and the medical profession.
The Canadian Medical Association does not at the present time voice an opinion either in favour of or adverse to health insurance.
The Canadian Medical Association is strenuously opposed to any form of state medicine which would tend to regiment or draft members of the medical profession into the ranks of state servants, controlled and salaried by the state, thus destroying the personal relation between doctor and patient.
The medical profession demands that it be relieved of the burden of gratuitously supplying medical services to the great majority of Canada's indigent and unemployed.
The Canadian Medical Association advocates the broadening of the federal health department's field of activities along the lines suggested at the 1935 meeting of the dominion health council.
The Canadian Medical Association recommends that before any form of health insurance is enacted by any legislative body, a royal commission be appointed to examine the whole question of health activities and medical services in Canada.
